stem: Find each function value, if possible.   g(x) = 2x² + 3x − 7    (a) g(−1)   (b) g(1)
title: Evaluate a quadratic function
steps: Replace every x with negative 1, in parentheses.
Negative 1 squared is 1. 2 minus 3 minus 7 is negative 8.
Now put in 1: 2 plus 3 minus 7 is negative 2.
If your version also asks for g of x plus 3, replace x with the whole expression x plus 3, then expand and combine.

stem: Find each function value, if possible.   f(x) = √(x + 9) + 3    (a) f(−9)   (b) f(0)
title: Evaluate a square root function
steps: Put in negative 9. The inside is 0, and the square root of 0 is 0, so f is 3.
Put in 0: the square root of 9 is 3, plus 3 is 6.
if the inside is negative → undefined
If the inside of a square root ever comes out negative, the value is undefined.

stem: Find each function value, if possible.   q(x) = 1/(x² − 25)    (a) q(0)   (b) q(5)
title: Evaluate a rational function
steps: You can't divide by 0, so q of 5 is undefined.

stem: Find each function value, if possible.   f(t) = |t|/t    (a) f(6)   (b) f(−4)
title: Evaluate |t|/t
steps: For a positive number, the absolute value is the same number, so you get 1.
For a negative number, the top is positive and the bottom is negative, so you get negative 1.
At 0 it would be 0 over 0, which is undefined.

stem: Find each function value, if possible.   f(r) = |r| + 3    (a) f(−2)   (b) f(0)
title: Evaluate an absolute value function
steps: The absolute value of negative 2 is 2. Add 3: 5.
The absolute value of 0 is 0, so f of 0 is 3.
If your version asks for f of r minus 3, replace r with r minus 3 inside the absolute value bars.

stem: Find each function value, if possible.   f(x) = { −3x − 3, x < 0;  x² + 2x − 1, x ≥ 0 }    (a) f(−2)   (b) f(0)
title: Evaluate a piecewise function
steps: First decide which piece to use. Negative 2 is less than 0, so use the first piece.
0 is not less than 0, but it is greater than or equal to 0, so use the second piece.

stem: Find each function value, if possible.   f(t) = 3 − √t    (a) f(9)   (b) f(1/4)
title: Evaluate 3 − √t
steps: The square root of 9 is 3, so f of 9 is 0.
The square root of one fourth is one half. 3 minus one half is 5 halves.

stem: Find the domain of the function.   f(t) = 1/t − 4/(t + 1)
title: Domain: two fractions
steps: A denominator can't be 0. The first denominator is t, and the second is t plus 1.
Every real number except negative 1 and 0. In interval notation, leave out those two numbers.

stem: Find the domain of the function.   f(x) = √(4 − x²)
title: Domain: √(c − x²)
steps: The inside of a square root can't be negative.
x squared is at most 4 when x is between negative 2 and 2.
Both ends are allowed, so use brackets.

stem: Find the domain of the function.   f(t) = 4/(t² − 6t)
title: Domain: a quadratic denominator
steps: Factor the denominator. It can't be 0.

stem: Find the domain of the function.   f(x) = √(x + 5)
title: Domain: √(x + a)
steps: The inside of the square root can't be negative.
Negative 5 is allowed, so it gets a bracket.

stem: Find the domain of the function.   f(s) = √(s − 1)/(s − 4)
title: Domain: a square root over a denominator
steps: Two rules: the square root needs s minus 1 to be at least 0, so s is at least 1.
And the denominator can't be 0, so s can't be 4.

stem: Find the domain of the function.   f(x) = ∛(x + 6)
title: Domain: a cube root
steps: ∛ of any real number is defined
You can take the cube root of a negative number. The cube root of negative 8 is negative 2.
So there are no restrictions: the domain is all real numbers.

stem: Find the domain of the function.   f(x) = 2x² + 5x + 2
title: Domain: a polynomial
steps: A polynomial has no denominators and no square roots, so nothing can go wrong.
The domain is all real numbers.

stem: Find the difference quotient and simplify your answer.   f(x) = −3x + 4,   (f(x + h) − f(x))/h,  h ≠ 0
title: Difference quotient: a linear function
steps: Replace x with x plus h.
Subtract f of x. Everything cancels except negative 3 h.
Divide by h: negative 3. For a line, the difference quotient is the slope.

stem: Find the difference quotient and simplify your answer.   f(x) = x² − 7x − 3,   (f(x + h) − f(x))/h,  h ≠ 0
title: Difference quotient: a quadratic
steps: f(x + h) = (x + h)² − 7(x + h) − 3 = x² + 2xh + h² − 7x − 7h − 3
Replace x with x plus h and expand. x plus h squared is x squared plus 2 x h plus h squared.
Subtract f of x. The x squared, negative 7 x, and negative 3 cancel.
Every term has an h, so divide each by h.

stem: Find the difference quotient and simplify your answer.   f(x) = x³ − 5x,   (f(x + h) − f(x))/h,  h ≠ 0
title: Difference quotient: a cubic
steps: Subtract f of x: the x cubed and the negative 5 x cancel.

stem: Find the difference quotient and simplify your answer.   f(t) = 1/t,   (f(t) − f(1))/(t − 1),  t ≠ 1
title: Difference quotient: 1/t
steps: Subtract the fractions with a common denominator of t.
Factor out negative 1 so that t minus 1 appears.
Dividing by t minus 1 cancels it, leaving negative 1 over t.

stem: Find the difference quotient and simplify your answer.   f(x) = x³,   (f(x) − f(−3))/(x + 3),  x ≠ −3
title: Difference quotient: (f(x) − f(c))/(x − c) for x³
steps: f of negative 3 is negative 27, so the top is x cubed plus 27.
Cancel x plus 3 with the denominator.

stem: Find the difference quotient and simplify your answer.   f(x) = x² + 5x,   (f(x) − f(1))/(x − 1),  x ≠ 1
title: Difference quotient: (f(x) − f(c))/(x − c) for a quadratic
steps: The top is x squared plus 5 x minus 6. Factor it. x minus 1 has to be a factor.
Cancel with the denominator: x plus 6.

stem: Find the difference quotient and simplify your answer.   f(x) = √x,   (f(x + h) − f(x))/h,  h ≠ 0
title: Difference quotient: a square root
steps: Multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate.
The top becomes x plus h minus x, which is h.
Cancel h. Leave the bottom as it is.

stem: Use the Vertical Line Test to determine whether the graph represents y as a function of x.
title: The Vertical Line Test
steps: imagine vertical lines sweeping across the graph
Picture vertical lines moving across the graph from left to right.
some vertical line crosses the graph twice → not a function
Here, some vertical line hits the graph in two places. That means one x value has two y values, so it is not a function.
every vertical line hits at most once → function
If every vertical line hits the graph at most once, it is a function. Circles, sideways parabolas, and vertical lines fail the test.

stem: Determine the open intervals on which the function is increasing, decreasing, or constant.   f(x) = |x + 3| + |x − 3|
title: Increasing and decreasing: a sum of absolute values
steps: Read the graph from left to right. On the left it falls, until x equals negative 3.
Between negative 3 and 3 it's flat, so it's constant.
After 3 it rises: increasing. Use open intervals: parentheses at the turning points.

stem: Determine the open intervals on which the function is increasing, decreasing, or constant.   f(x) = { x + 5, x ≤ −2;  3, −2 < x ≤ 3;  2x − 2, x > 3 }
title: Increasing and decreasing: a piecewise function
steps: x ≤ −2: x + 5 has slope 1 → increasing on (−∞, −2)
Look at each piece. The first piece has a positive slope, so it's increasing.
The middle piece is a horizontal line: constant.
Nothing falls, so it's never decreasing.

stem: Determine the open intervals on which the function is increasing, decreasing, or constant.   f(x) = x² + 4x
title: Increasing and decreasing: a parabola
steps: A parabola turns at its vertex. x is negative b over 2 a: negative 2.
a > 0 → opens up: falls, then rises
The x squared term is positive, so it opens up.
It falls until negative 2, then rises.

stem: Determine the open intervals on which the function is increasing, decreasing, or constant.   f(x) = x³ − 3x − 1
title: Increasing and decreasing: a cubic
steps: turning points from the graph: x = −1 and x = 1
Find where the graph turns around: x equals negative 1 and x equals 1.
Reading left to right, it rises, falls between the turning points, then rises again.

stem: Find the average rate of change of the function from x₁ = 0 to x₂ = 5.   f(x) = x² + 5x + 14
title: Average rate of change
steps: Find the function values at both x values.
The average rate of change is the change in y over the change in x: the slope between the two points.
50 over 5 is 10. For a linear function, the average rate of change is always just the slope.

stem: Write the most specific name of the function.   f(x) = x
title: Name a parent function
steps: f of x equals x is the identity function: the output is the same as the input. It's also linear, but identity is more specific.
c → constant;  mx + b → linear;  x² → squaring;  x³ → cubic
Others to know: a plain number is the constant function, m x plus b is linear, x squared is the squaring function, and x cubed is cubic.
√x → square root;  1/x → reciprocal;  |x| → absolute value;  ⟦x⟧ → greatest integer
Root x is the square root function, 1 over x is the reciprocal function, bars mean absolute value, and double brackets mean the greatest integer function.

stem: Evaluate the function for the given values.   f(x) = −⟦x + 4⟧ + 6    (a) f(21/5)   (b) f(−4)
title: Evaluate a greatest integer function
steps: The greatest integer of a number is the integer at or just below it. Always round down.
21 fifths is 4.2. Add 4: 8.2. Rounding down gives 8.
Then finish: negative 8 plus 6 is negative 2.
At negative 4, the inside is 0, so f is 0 plus 6, which is 6.
With negatives, rounding down goes away from 0: the greatest integer of negative 3.1 is negative 4.

stem: Find (f + g)(x) and (f − g)(x).   f(x) = x² + x − 5,   g(x) = x − 4
title: Add and subtract functions
steps: To add functions, add their expressions.
Combine like terms: x plus x is 2 x, and negative 5 minus 4 is negative 9.
To subtract, put g in parentheses and change the sign of every term in it.
The x terms cancel, and negative 5 plus 4 is negative 1.
If your version also asks for f over g, its domain leaves out where g is 0: x can't be 4.

stem: Find (a) f ∘ g, (b) g ∘ f, and (c) g ∘ g.   f(x) = −4x,   g(x) = x² − 2
title: Composition of functions
steps: f of g means put g inside f.
f multiplies its input by negative 4.
g of f puts negative 4 x into g. Square it, then subtract 2. Order matters: this is different.
g of g puts g into itself. Expand x squared minus 2, squared: x to the 4th minus 4 x squared plus 4. Then subtract 2.

stem: Find (a) f ∘ g and (b) g ∘ f, and the domain of each.   f(x) = √(x + 2),   g(x) = x²
title: Composition and domain: a square root
steps: f ∘ g = √(x² + 2) → domain: all real numbers
f of g puts x squared into the square root. x squared plus 2 is always positive, so every x works.
g of f squares the square root, which gives x plus 2.
but x must be in the domain of f: x ≥ −2 → [−2, ∞)
But x has to go into f first, and f needs x plus 2 to be at least 0. So the domain is negative 2 to infinity, even though x plus 2 looks like it works everywhere.

stem: Find (a) f ∘ g and (b) g ∘ f, and the domain of each.   f(x) = ∛(x − 3),   g(x) = x³ + 6
title: Composition and domain: a cube root
steps: f of g puts x cubed plus 6 into f.
g of f cubes the cube root, which undoes it.
Cube roots work for every real number, so both domains are all real numbers.

stem: Find (a) f ∘ g and (b) g ∘ f, and the domain of each.   f(x) = |x|,   g(x) = x + 4
title: Composition and domain: absolute value
steps: f of g puts x plus 4 inside the absolute value bars.
g of f adds 4 to the absolute value of x.
Nothing is ever undefined, so both domains are all real numbers.

stem: Find (a) f ∘ g and (b) g ∘ f, and the domain of each.   f(x) = 1/x,   g(x) = x + 8
title: Composition and domain: a reciprocal
steps: f of g puts x plus 8 in the denominator. It can't be 0, so x can't be negative 8.
g of f adds 8 to 1 over x. Now x can't be 0.
Write each domain in interval notation.

stem: Find (a) f ∘ g and (b) g ∘ f, and the domain of each.   f(x) = 4/(x² − 1),   g(x) = x + 1
title: Composition and domain: a rational function
steps: f of g puts x plus 1 into f. x plus 1 squared minus 1 simplifies to x squared plus 2 x.
The denominator factors as x times x plus 2, so x can't be 0 or negative 2.
g of f adds 1 to f. f's denominator is 0 at 1 and negative 1.

stem: g is related to a parent function. Identify the parent function f and describe the sequence of transformations from f to g.   g(x) = −2|x + 1| − 1
title: Describe transformations
steps: Start by naming the parent function: the absolute value function.
Inside the bars, plus 1 shifts the graph 1 unit to the left. Inside changes go the opposite way.
−2 in front → stretched by 2 and reflected in the x-axis
The 2 in front stretches it vertically by a factor of 2, and the negative sign reflects it in the x-axis.
Minus 1 at the end shifts it down 1.

stem: Write an equation for the function whose graph is described.   The shape of f(x) = x³, but shifted 2 units to the left and 3 units down, and then reflected in the x-axis.
title: Write an equation from a description
steps: Start with the parent function, x cubed.
Shifting left 2 means replace x with x plus 2.
Reflecting in the x-axis last means multiply the whole thing by negative 1.

stem: Use the Horizontal Line Test: does the function have an inverse function?
title: The Horizontal Line Test
steps: sweep horizontal lines across the graph
Picture horizontal lines moving up and down across the graph.
some horizontal line crosses more than once → no inverse
Here, a horizontal line hits the wave in more than one place. Two inputs give the same output, so the function isn't one-to-one and has no inverse function.
every horizontal line crosses at most once → inverse exists
If every horizontal line hits the graph at most once, the function is one-to-one and has an inverse. Lines, cubics, and square root curves pass. Parabolas and V shapes fail.

stem: Use the table of values for y = f(x) to find f⁻¹ at the given values.   x: −3, −1, 0, 2, 3    f(x): 13, 7, 4, −2, −5
title: Inverse values from a table
steps: The inverse switches inputs and outputs. To find f inverse of a number, find that number in the f of x row.
Negative 5 is under x equals 3, so f inverse of negative 5 is 3.
In the same way, negative 2 is under 2, and 13 is under negative 3.

stem: Are f and g inverse functions?   f(x) = √(x − 1),   g(x) = x² + 1, x ≥ 0
title: Verify inverse functions
steps: Put g into f. The 1s cancel, and the square root of x squared is x, since x is at least 0.
Put f into g. Squaring undoes the square root.
Both compositions give x, so f and g are inverses. If either one doesn't give x, they aren't.

stem: Find the inverse function of f.   f(x) = −5x + 8
title: Find the inverse of a linear function
steps: Write y for f of x, then switch x and y.
Solve for y: add 5 y and subtract x, then divide by 5.
So f inverse is negative one fifth x plus 8 fifths.

stem: Find the inverse function of f.   f(x) = x³ − 4
title: Find the inverse of a cubic
steps: Add 4, then take the cube root of both sides.

stem: Find the inverse function of f.   f(x) = (x + 4)², x ≥ −4
title: Find the inverse of a restricted square
steps: Switch x and y. The restriction makes f one-to-one, so the inverse exists.
Take the square root. Use the positive root, because the outputs of the inverse are at least negative 4.

stem: Find the inverse function of f.   f(x) = √(x − 1)
title: Find the inverse of a square root function
steps: The square root only gives outputs of 0 or more, so the inverse only uses x at least 0.

stem: Find the inverse function of f.   f(x) = 3/x
title: Find the inverse of k/x
steps: Multiply by y, then divide by x.

stem: Find the inverse function of f.   f(x) = (x + 5)/(x − 2)
title: Find the inverse of a rational function
steps: Multiply both sides by y minus 2 and distribute.
Get the y terms on one side, then factor out y.

stem: Determine whether the function has an inverse function. If it does, find the inverse.   f(x) = x⁴
title: A function with no inverse
steps: Test two inputs. Negative 1 and 1 both give 1.
Two different inputs give the same output, so f isn't one-to-one and has no inverse. Even powers, absolute values, and constants all do this.

stem: Determine whether the function has an inverse function. If it does, find the inverse.   f(x) = 4x + 4
title: A function with an inverse
steps: A line that isn't horizontal is one-to-one, so it has an inverse.
Switch x and y, then solve for y.

stem: Evaluate the function at the given value of x. Round to three decimal places.   f(x) = 600e^(0.035x),   x = 15
title: Evaluate an exponential function with e
steps: Put in 15 for x. Do the exponent first: 0.035 times 15 is 0.525.
On a calculator, use the e to the x key with 0.525.
Multiply by 600, and round to three decimal places at the very end.

stem: Evaluate the function at the given value of x. Round to three decimal places.   f(x) = 2ˣ,   x = 1.4
title: Evaluate an exponential function
steps: Type 2, the caret key, then 1.4. Round to three decimal places: 2.639.

stem: Which function is shown in the graph?
title: Match an exponential graph
steps: Start with the y-intercept. The graph crosses at negative 1.
Plain 2 to the x would cross at 1. A negative in front flips it to negative 1.
The graph also falls as you go right, which matches negative 2 to the x: the reflection of 2 to the x in the x-axis.

stem: Describe the transformations of the graph of f that yield the graph of g.   f(x) = (7/2)ˣ,   g(x) = (7/2)ˣ⁺³ + 1
title: Transformations of an exponential graph
steps: Adding 3 to x in the exponent shifts the graph 3 units left. Changes inside go the opposite way.
a shift 3 units left, then 1 unit up
So g is f shifted 3 units left and 1 unit up.

stem: Write the logarithmic equation in exponential form.   log (1/100) = −2
title: Logarithmic form to exponential form
steps: A log is an exponent. log base b of a equals c means b to the c equals a.
A log with no base written is base 10.
So 10 to the negative 2 equals 1 over 100.

stem: Write the logarithmic equation in exponential form.   ln 250 = 5.521…
title: Natural log to exponential form
steps: The base e goes to the power 5.521…, and that equals 250.

stem: Write the exponential equation in logarithmic form.   32¹ = 32
title: Exponential form to logarithmic form
steps: The base of the power becomes the base of the log, and the log equals the exponent.
Base 32, exponent 1, value 32: log base 32 of 32 equals 1.

stem: Write the exponential equation in logarithmic form.   e^(−0.693…) = 1/2
title: Exponential form with e to a natural log
steps: When the base is e, the log is the natural log, ln.
So ln of one half equals negative 0.693….

stem: Evaluate the logarithm at the given value of x without using a calculator.   f(x) = log₁₆ x,   x = 1/16
title: Evaluate a logarithm without a calculator
steps: A log asks a question: the base to what power gives this number?
A negative exponent gives the reciprocal, so 16 to the negative 1 is one sixteenth.

stem: Evaluate the logarithm at the given value of x without using a calculator.   g(x) = log_b x,   x = √b
title: Evaluate log_b of a power of b
steps: Write the square root as a power: b to the one half.
log base b of b to a power is just the power. The answer is one half.

stem: Find the domain, x-intercept, and vertical asymptote of the logarithmic function.   f(x) = log₅(x − 1) − 2
title: Domain, intercept, and asymptote of a log function
steps: The inside of a log must be positive. x minus 1 is positive when x is more than 1.
The vertical asymptote is where the inside equals 0: x equals 1.
For the x-intercept, set f equal to 0. Rewrite in exponential form: x minus 1 is 5 squared, so x is 26.

stem: Find the domain, x-intercept, and vertical asymptote of the logarithmic function.   f(x) = log₂(2 − x)
title: Domain of a reflected log function
steps: The inside must be positive. 2 minus x is positive when x is less than 2.
The inside is 0 at x equals 2.
The x-intercept: a log is 0 when its inside is 1. So 2 minus x is 1, and x is 1.

stem: Solve the exponential equation algebraically. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   2(10ˣ) = 24
title: Solve A(bˣ) = C
steps: First isolate the exponential: divide by 2.
Take the common log of both sides. log of 10 to the x is x.

stem: Solve the exponential equation algebraically. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   3ˣ + 3 = 23
title: Solve bˣ + c = d
steps: Take ln of both sides. The exponent comes down in front.

stem: Solve the exponential equation algebraically. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   7¹⁻ˣ = 400
title: Solve b^(p − x) = C
steps: Take ln of both sides. The whole exponent, 1 minus x, comes down.

stem: Solve the exponential equation algebraically. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   500e^(2x) = 100
title: Solve A e^(kx) = C
steps: Take ln of both sides: ln of e to the 2 x is 2 x.

stem: Solve the exponential equation algebraically. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   7 − 3eˣ = 1
title: Solve a − c eˣ = d
steps: Get the e to the x term alone: subtract 1 and add 3 e to the x, or move terms in whichever order you like.

stem: Solve the exponential equation algebraically. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   eˣ = e^(x² − 2)
title: Solve with the One-to-One Property
steps: Same base on both sides, so the exponents are equal.
Rearrange into a quadratic and factor.

stem: Solve the exponential equation algebraically. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   e²ˣ − 8eˣ + 15 = 0
title: Solve a quadratic in eˣ
steps: e to the 2 x is e to the x, squared. So it's a quadratic in e to the x.

stem: Solve the exponential equation algebraically. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   1/(1 − eˣ) = 5
title: Solve 1/(1 − eˣ) = c
steps: Take the reciprocal of both sides.
Solve for e to the x.

stem: Solve the exponential equation algebraically. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   400/(1 + e²ˣ) = 10
title: Solve a logistic-type equation
steps: Multiply both sides by 1 plus e to the 2 x, then divide by 10.

stem: Solve the exponential equation algebraically. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   (1 + 0.08/4)^(4t) = 4
title: Solve a compound interest equation
steps: The base is 1 plus 0.02, which is 1.02.
Take ln of both sides. The exponent 4 t comes down.
Divide. Use a calculator only at the end.

stem: Solve the logarithmic equation algebraically, if possible. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   ln x = −3
title: Solve ln x = c
steps: Rewrite in exponential form: x is e to the negative 3.

stem: Solve the logarithmic equation algebraically, if possible. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   2.1 = ln 2x
title: Solve c = ln(ax)
steps: Rewrite in exponential form: 2 x equals e to the 2.1.

stem: Solve the logarithmic equation algebraically, if possible. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   4 − 4 ln x = 8
title: Solve a + b ln x = d
steps: Divide by negative 4, then rewrite in exponential form.

stem: Solve the logarithmic equation algebraically, if possible. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   log 4z = 1
title: Solve log(az) = c
steps: A common log has base 10. Rewrite in exponential form.

stem: Solve the logarithmic equation algebraically, if possible. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   4 log(x − 6) = 11
title: Solve k log(x − h) = d
steps: Divide by 4 to isolate the log.

stem: Solve the logarithmic equation algebraically, if possible. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   log(5x − 3) = log(x − 1)
title: Solve log(A) = log(B), and check
steps: The logs are equal, so the insides are equal.
Always check: the inside of a log must be positive. Here it's negative.
So the equation has no solution.

stem: Solve the logarithmic equation algebraically, if possible. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   log x + log(x + 2) = log(x + 6)
title: Solve with the product rule, and check
steps: Combine the left side with the product rule.
Set the insides equal and rearrange.
x = −3 makes log x undefined → x = 2
Check each one. Negative 3 can't go into log x, so only 2 works.

stem: Solve the logarithmic equation algebraically, if possible. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   log₃ x − log₃(x − 3) = 2
title: Solve with the quotient rule
steps: Multiply by x minus 3 and solve. 27 eighths makes both insides positive, so it works.

stem: Solve the logarithmic equation algebraically, if possible. Approximate the result to three decimal places, if necessary.   ln(x + 2) = ln(x − 1) − ln(x + 1)
title: A log equation with no solution
steps: Combine the right side with the quotient rule.
Set the insides equal and multiply by x plus 1.

stem: Evaluate (if possible) the sine, cosine, and tangent of the real number.   t = 5π/3
title: Sine, cosine, and tangent from the unit circle
steps: Find 5 pi over 3 on the unit circle. It's in the fourth quadrant, with reference angle pi over 3, at the point one half, negative root 3 over 2.
sin t = y = −√3/2;  cos t = x = 1/2
Sine is the y-coordinate and cosine is the x-coordinate.
Tangent is y over x: negative root 3. If x is 0, tangent is undefined.

stem: Use the value of the trigonometric function to evaluate the indicated functions.   sin t = −1/9    (a) sin(−t)   (b) csc(−t)
title: Sine is odd
steps: Sine is an odd function: sine of negative t is the opposite of sine of t.
Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine: 1 over one ninth is 9.

stem: Use the value of the trigonometric function to evaluate the indicated functions.   cos(−t) = 5/9    (a) cos t   (b) sec(−t)
title: Cosine is even
steps: Cosine is an even function: cosine of negative t equals cosine of t.
Secant is the reciprocal of cosine: 9 fifths.

stem: Use the value of the trigonometric function to evaluate the indicated functions.   cos t = −3/5    (a) cos(π − t)   (b) cos(t + π)
title: cos(π − t) and cos(t + π)
steps: π − t: reflect across the y-axis → x changes sign
On the unit circle, pi minus t is the mirror image of t across the y-axis. The x-coordinate changes sign.
So cosine of pi minus t is negative cosine t: 3 fifths.
t + π: the opposite point → both signs change → cos(t + π) = 3/5
t plus pi is directly across the circle, so both coordinates change sign. Cosine of t plus pi is also 3 fifths.

stem: Use the value of the trigonometric function to evaluate the indicated functions.   sin t = −4/5    (a) sin(π − t)   (b) sin(t + π)
title: sin(π − t) and sin(t + π)
steps: π − t: reflect across the y-axis → same y
Pi minus t is the mirror image of t across the y-axis. The y-coordinate stays the same.
So sine of pi minus t is negative 4 fifths.
t + π: the opposite point → sin(t + π) = −sin t = 4/5
t plus pi is directly across the circle, so the y-coordinate changes sign: 4 fifths.

stem: Evaluate the trigonometric function using its period as an aid.   cos (7π/3)
title: Use the period to evaluate
steps: Cosine repeats every 2 pi, so you can subtract 2 pi without changing the value.
Write 2 pi as 6 pi over 3 and subtract.
Cosine of pi over 3 is one half.

stem: Find the period and amplitude.   y = 2 sin(πx/4)
title: Amplitude and period
steps: y = a sin bx: amplitude = |a|, period = 2π/b
For a sine or cosine graph, the amplitude is the absolute value of a, and the period is 2 pi over b.
b is pi over 4. Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal: 8.

stem: Write an equation for the sine function y = a sin(bx − c) + d (with a > 0 and b > 0) that has the given characteristics.   Amplitude: 2;   period: 2π/3;   phase shift: π/2 to the right;   vertical shift: 4 up
title: Write a sine or cosine equation
steps: b is 2 pi over the period: 3.
The phase shift is c over b, so c is b times the phase shift. Shifting right makes c positive.
d is the vertical shift, 4 up. Put it all together.

stem: Find a, b, and c for the function f(x) = a sin(bx − c) so that the graph of f matches the figure. (One full period starts at x = π/2.)
title: Find a, b, and c from a graph
steps: The graph goes up 3 and down 3 from the middle, so a is 3.
One full cycle is 4 pi long, so b is 2 pi over 4 pi: one half.
starts at π/2 → c/b = π/2 → c = (1/2)(π/2) = π/4
A cycle starts at pi over 2, so the phase shift c over b is pi over 2. c is one half times pi over 2, which is pi over 4.

stem: Find the period of the function.   y = −tan 3x
title: Period of tangent or cotangent
steps: tan and cot have period π → period = π/b
Tangent and cotangent repeat every pi, not 2 pi. So the period is pi over b.
b is 3, so the period is pi over 3. The negative in front doesn't change the period.

stem: Find the period of the function.   y = (1/3) csc(πx)
title: Period of secant or cosecant
steps: sec and csc have period 2π → period = 2π/b
Secant and cosecant repeat every 2 pi, like cosine and sine.
b is pi, so the period is 2. The one third in front doesn't change the period.

stem: Evaluate the expression without using a calculator. Give the answer in radians (or write "not possible").   arccos (−√3/2)
title: Evaluate an inverse trig function
steps: arccos gives an angle between 0 and pi. arcsin and arctan give angles between negative pi over 2 and pi over 2.
cos θ = −√3/2 with θ in [0, π] → θ = 5π/6
Which angle in that range has cosine negative root 3 over 2? 5 pi over 6.
arcsin or arccos of a number outside [−1, 1] → not possible
If the number is bigger than 1 or less than negative 1, arcsin and arccos aren't possible. arctan works for any number.

stem: Use the properties of inverse trigonometric functions to evaluate the expression.   arccos(cos (4π/3))
title: arccos(cos x): check the range
steps: arccos(cos x) = x only if x is in [0, π]
Inverse undoes the function only when x is in the inverse's output range. For arccos, that's 0 to pi.
4π/3 is not in [0, π] → evaluate inside first
4 pi over 3 is too big, so work from the inside out.
Cosine of 4 pi over 3 is negative one half. arccos of negative one half is 2 pi over 3.

stem: Use the properties of inverse trigonometric functions to evaluate the expression, or write "not possible".   sin(arcsin 0.3)
title: sin(arcsin x)
steps: sin(arcsin x) = x for every x in [−1, 1]
The function undoes its inverse whenever the inverse is defined.
0.3 is between negative 1 and 1, so the answer is 0.3. If the number were outside, like negative root 3 in arccos, it would not be possible.

stem: Find the exact value of the expression. (Hint: sketch a right triangle.)   sin(arccos (−5/13))
title: Exact value with a right triangle
steps: θ = arccos(−5/13) → cos θ = −5/13, θ in [0, π]
Name the inside angle theta. Its cosine is negative 5 over 13, and arccos puts it between 0 and pi: the second quadrant.
Draw the triangle: adjacent negative 5, hypotenuse 13. The other side is 12, positive in quadrant two.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse: 12 over 13.

stem: Write an algebraic expression that is equivalent to the given expression. (Hint: sketch a right triangle.)   cot(tan⁻¹ (x/4))
title: Write an algebraic expression with a triangle
steps: θ = tan⁻¹(x/4) → tan θ = x/4 = opp/adj
Name the angle theta. Its tangent is x over 4, so the opposite side is x and the adjacent side is 4.
The hypotenuse is the square root of x squared plus 16.
Cotangent is adjacent over opposite: 4 over x.

stem: Find all solutions of the equation in the interval [0, 2π):   2 csc x − 4 sin x = 0
title: Solve a trig equation in [0, 2π)
steps: 2 csc x − 4 sin x = 0 → × sin x: 2 − 4 sin² x = 0
Get everything in terms of one function. Here, multiply by sine x, since cosecant is 1 over sine.
Solve for sine x. Don't forget the plus or minus.
Find every angle from 0 to 2 pi with each value, using the unit circle.
other strategies: use identities (sec² = 1 + tan²), divide by cos x, or factor
Other problems may need an identity, dividing by cosine, or factoring like a quadratic. Always get one trig function, then use the unit circle.

stem: Solve the equation:   cot² x + cot x = 0
title: Solve a trig equation by factoring
steps: Factor like a quadratic. Don't divide by cot x, or you'll lose solutions.
Set each factor equal to 0 and find the angles in one turn.
Cotangent repeats every pi, so add n pi to get all solutions. Pairs that are pi apart combine.

stem: Find all solutions of the equation in the interval [0, 2π). Round to four decimal places.   5 cos² x − 1 = 0
title: Solve a trig equation with a calculator
steps: Isolate the trig function, then take the square root: plus or minus.
In radian mode, arccos gives one angle. Cosine is also positive in quadrant four: 2 pi minus that angle.
Do the same with the negative value.
List all four, rounded to four decimal places.
